title: Policy-driven adaptive prefetching — architecture review notes
content:
Meeting: Architecture review — Policy-driven adaptive prefetching
Date: 2025-11-12
Location: Zoom + #eng-serving-runtime
Attendees: Ava Martinez (chair), Rohit Singh, Mei Chen, Liam O'Connor, Priya Desai, Spencer Holt (observability), Carla Vega (SRE), Jonah Patel (product)

Purpose:
We reviewed a proposed architecture for a policy-driven adaptive prefetching layer in the serving runtime. Goal: reduce cold-KV/cache and model-weight fetch latency for common conversational patterns while controlling cost and avoiding undue resource churn. This is not a replacement for existing KV prefix caching; it sits above the hotstore/cache hierarchy and coordinates prefetch decisions using routing and SLO policy signals.

Agenda:
- Quick recap of latency tail problem and recent p99 regressions (Spencer)
- Proposal walkthrough (Ava + Rohit)
- Design alternatives and trade-offs (group)
- Observability and simulation plan (Spencer + Mei)
- Rollout strategy and failure modes (Carla + Liam)
- Action items and owners

Recap of problem:
- In the last two quarters we observed correlated p99 spikes when conversational workloads shift (longer multi-turn sessions, sudden bursts from a few tenants).
- Root cause analysis indicates two main contributors: KV cache misses for conversation prefixes and model weight page-ins on heterogeneous accelerators during variant switchover.
- Current reactive prefetch (on-request) produces tail amplification under load and causes latency SLO breaches during traffic spikes.

Proposal summary (Policy-driven Adaptive Prefetching):
1) Policy layer: prefetch decisions derived from routing and SLO policies. Inputs include tenant SLO class, route priority, recent sequence-length distribution, and model-variant cost/duty cycles.
2) Heuristic engine: lightweight rules run in the control plane that infer near-term prefetch candidates (conversation prefixes, KV shards, weight segments). Rules are deterministic initially (windowed frequency, sticky session detection, and predicted next-token-affinity) with a tunable confidence score.
3) Prefetch executors: worker-tier that prefetches into the hotstore/edge cache and optionally warms GPU memory for selected weight shards (on supported HW). Executors respect budget tokens from runtime (crediting) to avoid resource exhaustion.
4) Feedback loop: runtime telemetry (misses, prefetch hit rate, added latency, resource usage) flows back to refine policy thresholds.
5) Fail-safe: prefetching is scoped by tenant/resource class and can be disabled or limited via per-tenant quotas and an emergency kill-switch that SRE can toggle.

Design goals and constraints:
- Goal: measurably reduce p95/p99 for conversational flows that are cacheable without raising steady-state cost > 8% for the tenant.
- Must be incremental and observable; every prefetch ticket is tagged and traced end-to-end.
- No tight coupling to model internals; we operate at shard/segment granularity that is compatible with quantized and sharded model variants.
- Support hosted, dedicated, and private modes — private deployments can opt-in and configure different budgets.

Alternatives considered (and why rejected for now):
A) Always-on aggressive prefetching: simpler but blows costs and increases eviction churn in multi-tenant hosts — rejected.
B) Full ML predictor trained on historical sequences: higher precision but longer development and operational risk; recommended as a mid-term enhancement after rule-engine proves stable.
C) Move all prefetching to client-side SDKs (push model): unworkable for enterprise customers where SDK modifications are slow and private deployments cannot rely on SDK updates.

Interaction with existing components:
- KV prefix cache: policy layer issues prefetch writes into the hotstore API (same interface used by runtime cache-fill). We will add an explicit "prefetch provenance" metadata tag to avoid evicting these entries prematurely.
- Model weight manager: executors request weight shard loading via the compilation/kernel selection layer. For model variants that support partial page-in, we will request prioritized load for the top-k layers indicated by the rule engine.
- Router/policy service: integrates with existing routing policy data (SLO class, priority) and subscribes to per-tenant traffic summaries.

Telemetry and metrics (proposal):
- Prefetch hit rate (by tenant/route/model-variant)
- Delta in p50/p95/p99 latency for prefetch-targeted requests
- Resource overhead (network IO, hotstore ingress, GPU memory pressure) attributable to prefetching
- Eviction churn (prefetch-originated entries vs reactive entries)
- Cost delta estimate per tenant (tokens/week equivalent)
Success criteria for canary:
- p99 for targeted workloads reduces by >= 20% without steady-state cost increase > 8% for the canary cohort.
- No increase in incident rate tied to memory pressure or OOMs during a 2-week canary run.

Security and privacy notes:
- Prefetch decisions are purely meta-data driven — no additional user content is retained beyond existing flow-level metadata. We will document behavior in the privacy registry and include opt-out hooks for regulated tenants.

Rollout plan:
Phase 0 — simulation (2 weeks): use replay harness (INF-2384) to simulate prefetch rules against a 30-day traffic window and produce cost/benefit projections. (Owner: Mei)
Phase 1 — read-only prefetch tagging (1 week): run executors in dry-run that tag would-be-prefetch candidates and emit telemetry but do not write to hotstore. (Owner: Rohit)
Phase 2 — limited canary (2 weeks): enable prefetch writes for 5% of traffic on dedicated capacity with strict quotas. Monitor metrics and safety signals. (Owners: Liam + Carla)
Phase 3 — progressive ramp (4 weeks): expand to larger cohort and tune thresholds; enable optional weight-warm for selected model-variants.
Phase 4 — GA opt-in (after success and product review): expose per-tenant controls in Console under "Performance optimizations". (Owner: Jonah)

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Over-prefetching causes eviction storms: mitigation = rapid quota throttling and revert to dry-run for affected hosts.
- Prefetch-induced GPU OOMs: executor checks memory headroom; if memory pressure > threshold, disable weight-warm and fallback to KV-only prefetch.
- Misclassification of sessions leading to wasted IO: initially run conservative thresholds and require cross-signal agreement (frequency + sticky-session confidence).

Decisions made at this meeting:
1) Proceed with the rule-based heuristic engine as phase 0 and 1; postpone ML predictor until after stable telemetry. (Decision: APPROVED)
2) Implement prefetch provenance tagging in hotstore and evictions policy changes to favor recent reactive hits over stale prefetch entries. (Decision: APPROVED)
3) Enable per-tenant opt-out and quota controls exposed via internal API and Console. (Decision: APPROVED)

Open questions (to resolve in follow-up):
- Exact credit accounting model for prefetch tokens (network vs memory vs GPU time). (Owner: Spencer, due 2025-11-20)
- How to version and roll back weight-warm strategies for different quantization formats safely. (Owner: Rohit, due 2025-11-21)
- Security review checklist for private deployments (Carla + legal). (Owner: Carla, due 2025-11-19)

Action items (owners and due dates):
- Mei: run replay simulation and produce a metric snapshot and cost projection (INF-2384) — due 2025-11-19.
- Rohit: implement dry-run tagging in hotstore client and add provenance field to cache entries — PR referenced in linked_artifacts — due 2025-11-17.
- Liam + Carla: prepare canary run playbook and SLO safety hooks; add automation for emergency kill-switch — due 2025-11-24.
- Jonah: draft Console UX for opt-in controls and tenant-level reporting — due 2025-11-26.
- Ava: coordinate follow-up review once simulation results are in and schedule a 60-minute sync for 2025-11-20.

Notes and rationale (additional context):
- The group prefers starting conservative: rule-based prefetch allows quick iteration, easier debugging, and clearer failure explanations to SRE and customers.
- There is consensus that weight warming should be optional and gated behind explicit model-variant compatibility checks to avoid cross-variant interference.
- Observability investments (traces + lineage tags) are mandatory before any write-enabled canary.

Appendix: example rules (draft)
- Rule A: sticky-session + sequence-length > 8 + last-5-turns repeated prefix freq >= 3 => prefetch top N prefix KV shards with confidence score 0.7
- Rule B: tenant SLO class = gold AND route priority = high AND expected tokens/min > 120 => prefetch latest KV + warm top-2 weight shards (if memory headroom >= 30%)
- Rule C: workstation/dev tenants = false => do not prefetch to conserve dev quotas

End of notes.
